summary: Texas's 1872 cast-iron tower at the north side of Galveston Bay's entrance: storms of 1900 and 1915, dark since 1933, privately owned and closed.

lens.where: Smithsonian National Museum of American History (LighthouseFriends)

access.note: Privately owned. Grounds and tower closed to visitors.

facts.agency: Private owners, descendants of the Boyt family (Bolivar Point Lighthouse Foundation)

events.note: Station established; keeper's dwelling finished April 1852; lamps in by Christmas 1852
Third-order lens and 24 feet of tower sections added after harbor pilots' complaints
First tower destroyed or dismantled during the Civil War; sources differ on how
Temporary 34-foot wooden tower with fourth-order lens lit 5 August 1865
Present cast-iron tower, 117 feet above mean high water
Second-order lens installed to replace the third-order lens
8 September 1900 hurricane; over 120 people sheltered in the tower
Fixed second-order light changed to flashing third-order
16-17 August 1915 hurricane; keeper's dwelling washed off its foundation, other buildings destroyed; per LighthouseFriends the light went dark for two nights after the oil ran out
Shelled in dense fog by Fort San Jacinto guns during target practice (15 November 1917)
Two frame dwellings on high iron columns and a new oil house
Property transferred to the War Department
Sold as surplus property; the sources name the buyer differently
Tower appears in the television drama My Sweet Charlie
Texas Historical Commission registers it as a historic landmark
Bolivar Point Lighthouse Foundation formed by descendants of the first private owners
Lantern room removed by crane on 15 May 2023 for restoration

corrections.why: The USLHS record and LighthouseFriends date the first light to 1852; the 1855 date is not supported by any source read for this story.
The present tower was first lit on 19 November 1872 (LighthouseFriends, the Foundation); the Handbook of Texas also dates it to 1872.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record gives 1852 and 1855. The USLHS record gives 1852 as the year established, and LighthouseFriends says the lamps were in by Christmas 1852. TSHA's 1855 mention is a survey line-up, not a first-light date. The 1855 entry is not supported.
The record's 1873 build year from Rowlett's conflicts with 1872 in LighthouseFriends, TSHA and the Foundation. The 1872 date is used.

notes_for_editor: Sources disagree and the story says so: the first light (1852 vs 1855), the Civil War fate of the first tower (TSHA says destroyed by Confederates; LighthouseFriends says dismantled, with the iron's use assumed), the 1947 buyer (Elmer V. Boyt per LighthouseFriends; E. W. Boyt interests per TSHA; E. V. Boyt and sister Ila Maxwell per the Foundation), and the number of refugees in 1900 (125 Foundation, over 120 LighthouseFriends) and 1915 (fifty Putnam, sixty LighthouseFriends and the Galveston Daily News reprint, 61 Foundation). The 1915 duration of the dark light is two nights per LighthouseFriends; the newspaper reprint does not give a number. The NRHP nomination (NRIS 77001445) is not digitised (npgallery placeholder) and the NARA catalogue is off-limits, so the 1977 NRHP listing is not sourced here; the Texas Historical Commission listing rests on the TSHA entry. The current characteristic and the 1907 signature are not verified from a Coast Guard List of Lights. The Galveston Daily News account was read in the Lighthouse Service Bulletin reprint, not in the newspaper; no Chronicling America page was read for this station. The roster was matched by position (0.78 km). The archive prints the 1906 first assistant as 'Mrs. J.B. Caliborne'; the story keeps that spelling. The index entries for commendations were matched by position on the Bulletin index (pages 181-183) and name the commendations but not the storm. The 1917 shelling rests on three secondary sources (LighthouseFriends, TSHA, Foundation); the Bulletin index does not list it and no primary record was found in the corpus. The 1901 Board report was checked for the rejected bids only; the story does not claim the work was done by hired labour. Wikipedia was used for leads only and is not cited. Fact-check 2026-10-22: the index page (PDF p. 4) was read from the page image; the commendations sit on p. 182 and the storm account is listed at pp. 182-183. The Galveston Daily News reprint runs PDF pp. 37-38 in the 1915 Bulletin: the 9.15 p.m. passage, the neck-deep water, the rope and the two dark nights are on p. 38. The 1918 dwellings are listed as completed work in the Commissioner's report for the fiscal year ended 30 June 1918 (p. 42); the story no longer dates them to 1917.
